title: The Coefficients parameters
$comment: Every default below was read from the vendored micropolisJS source at commit f13a1624 and matches it exactly. A default that disagrees with the engine is the worst possible bug in this sandbox, because the whole sandbox is an argument about what the defaults are. Slider granularity is x-step, never multipleOf - see the note in bathtub's schema for why. Property order is the panel's reading order: the two contested constants first, then the rest of the rules, then the run, then how it is drawn.

crime_base.title: Crime base
crime_base.description: The line is: crime = 128 - land value + population density - police. This number is the 128. It sets how much crime a place has before anything about that place is taken into account, and everything else is a correction to it. Nothing in the engine derived it and no data was fitted to produce it; it is a constant somebody typed in 1989 and it has been copied forward ever since. Move it and watch the whole map change at once - then notice that population falls too, because low land value raises crime and high crime lowers land value, and the engine closes that loop on purpose.

crime_land_value_weight.title: Weight on land value
crime_land_value_weight.description: How strongly cheap land is taken to produce crime. The engine's own value is 1, meaning one point of land value cancels exactly one point of crime - a one-to-one exchange rate between property prices and offences that no study anywhere established. Set it to 0 and the model stops claiming that poverty causes crime; the rest of the simulation carries on without complaint, which is worth seeing.

crime_police_weight.title: Weight on police
crime_police_weight.description: How strongly police presence suppresses crime. The engine's value is 1, and police cover is on a 0-1000 scale while crime is on 0-250 - so a station at full strength does not reduce crime, it erases it. Policing in this model has no diminishing return, no displacement of crime elsewhere, and no upper limit on what it can achieve.

land_value_centre_base.title: Land value at the centre
land_value_centre_base.description: The value of land at the city centre, before distance is subtracted. The engine's 34 is then shifted left twice, which multiplies it by four, so the real ceiling is 136. Raising this raises the whole surface without changing its shape.

land_value_distance_divisor.title: Distance divisor
land_value_distance_divisor.description: The whole line is: land value = 34 - distance from the city centre / 2. That is a bid-rent gradient, in one statement, with nothing else in it. This number is how fast value falls as you walk away from the middle. Because the model is written this way, no city it can produce is polycentric, and no place far from the centre can be expensive - not because that was tested and found true, but because there is nowhere in the code to express it. Turn the divisor up and the gradient flattens; the city gets richer and less centralised, and it still cannot have two centres.

max_traffic_distance.title: How far traffic looks
max_traffic_distance.description: A zone counts as having access to jobs if a random walk along the roads finds a destination within this many steps. There is no route planning, no journey time, no congestion feeding back into the choice, and nobody deciding where to go - the walk is random and the only question is whether it arrives. On a compact grid like the starting city almost every destination is close, so this control does less here than it would on a sprawling map. That is itself worth knowing about a parameter.

smooth_passes.title: Police smoothing passes
smooth_passes.description: How a police station's influence spreads: by blurring the map of station positions, three times, and calling the result coverage. That is the entire theory of how a service reaches a neighbourhood - a convolution, with the radius set by a repeat count rather than by a distance, a response time, or a road. Set it to 0 and cover collapses to the stations themselves, and crime rises everywhere else.

birth_rate.title: Birth rate
birth_rate.description: Population growth per turn, as a flat share of the residential population. There is no age, no household, no migration in or out, and nobody arriving because the city got better. Demography in this model is one multiplication.

ext_market_index.title: Outside demand
ext_market_index.description: Demand for what the city's industry makes, from everywhere that is not the city. It is one of three numbers, chosen by the difficulty setting, and it never changes for any other reason. The world outside is a constant.

seed.title: Seed
seed.description: The starting number for every random choice the simulation makes. The rules and the starting city are identical for every seed; this is the only thing that differs between the runs on the divergence chart. Change it and you get a different city out of the same model, which is the point that chart exists to make.

run_count.title: Runs to compare
run_count.description: How many seeds the divergence chart runs, headlessly, in the background. Each one starts from the same city under the same rules. The spread between them at the end is not noise in a measurement - it is what this model does.

ticks.title: Steps per run
ticks.description: How many steps each comparison run takes. One step is one phase of the sixteen-phase cycle, so a full turn of the city's clock is sixteen of them.

layer.title: Layer over the city
layer.description: Which layer to wash over the city, tile for tile. 'none' follows the rotation - the wash tracks whatever layer the cycle most recently wrote. All fifteen are drawn small in the rail regardless; click one there to pin it.
